name: 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿𐎠
note: Old Persian, the language of the Achaemenid kings from Darius I (522-486 BC), in its own cuneiform syllabary (U+103A0-U+103DF), left to right, with the word divider replaced by spaces so long lines can wrap. The script writes a consonant with an inherent a, or with i or u where a sign exists (di, mu, vi...); the words here follow the inscriptions' spelling rules: a long ā adds the a sign, i and u are written with their vowel signs after the consonant, a consonant ending a syllable takes its a-sign, and a word ending in a short a adds nothing. Spellings are normalized the way the grammars cite them (Kent, Schmitt), so Exported Python prints that transliteration instead of the signs, with th for θ. The words were made by a model, not read by a scholar of the language: treat the grammar as approximate. The inscriptions (Behistun, Persepolis, Naqsh-i Rustam, Susa) keep a narrow vocabulary, so modern ideas are descriptive coinages on attested words, used the same way everywhere: aθanga (stone) for block, framānā (command, order) for program, paθi (path) for script, paraiti (going forth) for a run, with paraidiy (go forth!) on the Run button, patikara (image, likeness) for model, bandaka (vassal, servant) for agent, abijāra (instrument) for tool, patiparsā (read, examine) for review, fratama nipištam (first writing) for draft, kartam (what was done) for the result, vitara (what changes) for variable, dipiš (inscription, document) for file, ganza (treasury) for folder, hamārakara (reckoner) for computer, raucanāma (book of days) for calendar, rāstā (row) for list, handugā (statement) for record, dašta (hand, part) for a record's field, dāma (net) for the web, pavastā (clay envelope) for page, hamāraka (counter) for token, kilīda (key) for key, nidāna (deposit) for checkpoint, frastam (what is sent) for message, dipiš frasta (sent document) for email, citra (form, seed) for picture and ušī (understanding) for memory. Commands are in the imperative singular, as the kings address the reader. Field names, status values, settings, commands and product names stay as they are, in Latin letters, as in the other languages. The page serves the Noto Sans Old Persian font named in "font". Blockly has no Old Persian locale, so "blockly" is "en" and blocklyMsg holds the words of Blockly's own blocks.
